Title: Built in Babylon
Text: Nebuchadnezzar II orders the gate built as part of the Processional Way and dedicates it to the goddess Ishtar.

Title: Excavation
Text: A German Oriental Society team under Robert Koldewey excavates Babylon. Of the 120 lions along the Processional Way, 118 are taken.

Title: Shipped to Berlin
Text: The glazed brick fragments are numbered, packed into barrels, carried down the Euphrates and loaded onto German ships for Berlin.

Title: Rebuilt in the Pergamonmuseum
Text: After years of desalinating and piecing together fragments with newly fired bricks, the smaller front gate is rebuilt inside the new museum. The larger rear gate stays in storage.

Title: War
Text: The museum closes during the Second World War, and the gate is damaged by bombs.

Title: Iraq asks for its return
Text: The Iraqi government petitions Germany to return the gate, notably in 2002 and 2009. The gate remains in Berlin.

Title: Behind closed doors
Text: The Pergamonmuseum has been closed since October 2023. The wing with the Ishtar Gate will stay closed even after the partial reopening planned for June 2027.

Title: Built on the acropolis of Pergamon
Text: King Eumenes II builds the altar with its frieze of gods fighting giants.

Title: Reused as building stone
Text: With the rise of Christianity the altar loses its function; parts are broken up to fortify the acropolis.

Title: Excavation
Text: German engineer Carl Humann and Alexander Conze excavate the acropolis. The new German Empire wants Greek originals to rival the British Museum.

Title: Shipped to Berlin
Text: Under an agreement between the Ottoman Empire and the German government, the relief panels are taken to Berlin's royal collections.

Title: A museum named after it
Text: The altar becomes the centrepiece of the new Pergamonmuseum.

Title: War trophy in Leningrad
Text: At the end of the war the Red Army takes the panels to the Soviet Union, where they are kept in the Hermitage depot. They return to East Berlin in 1959.

Title: Turkey asks for its return
Text: Turkey's culture minister demands the return of the altar and other artefacts.

Title: Out of view since 2014
Text: The altar hall has been closed since 2014 and the whole museum since 2023; a partial reopening is planned for June 2027.

Title: Built at the market of Miletus
Text: A two-storey marble gate is built at the entrance to the southern market.

Title: Destroyed by an earthquake
Text: The gate collapses and lies in ruins for centuries.

Title: Excavation
Text: Theodor Wiegand's team excavates the gate during German excavations at Miletus (1899–1911).

Title: Shipped to Berlin
Text: The fragments are transported to Berlin. Impressed by Wiegand's models, Kaiser Wilhelm II orders a full-size reconstruction 'like a theatre backdrop'.

Title: Rebuilt with concrete and steel
Text: Over 750 tons of fragments are assembled, filled out with brick, cement and steel. Critics accuse the museum of presenting a largely new structure as an original.

Title: Bombed and restored
Text: Bombing destroys the roof above the gate and part of the structure collapses; it is restored in 1952–1954 and again in the 2000s.

Title: An unfinished palace
Text: Caliph al-Walid II probably commissions the winter palace; after his murder the building is abandoned.

Title: A gift between emperors
Text: Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II gives the facade to his ally, the German Emperor Wilhelm II.

Title: Shipped to Berlin
Text: A large part of the facade is brought to the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum (today's Bode Museum) and rebuilt as a 33-metre wall.

Title: Moved to the Pergamonmuseum
Text: The facade is reassembled in the Pergamonmuseum, where it becomes a centrepiece of the Museum of Islamic Art.

Title: Damaged in the war
Text: The facade is seriously damaged during the bombing of Berlin.

Title: Two halves of one palace
Text: The plain walls of the palace still stand south of Amman, while its carved entrance is in a closed museum in Berlin.

Title: Made in Thutmose's workshop
Text: The sculptor Thutmose makes the painted limestone bust of Queen Nefertiti.

Title: Found in the sand
Text: A team funded by the German Oriental Society and led by Ludwig Borchardt finds the bust. 'You cannot describe it with words. You must see it,' Borchardt writes.

Title: Division of the finds
Text: The finds are divided with the French-run Egyptian Antiquities Service. Borchardt shows an unflattering photo, calls the bust gypsum instead of limestone, and keeps it wrapped in a box.

Title: Kept secret in Berlin
Text: The bust goes to the excavation's sponsor James Simon and then to the museum, but is hidden from the public at Borchardt's request until 1924.

Title: Unveiled, and claimed
Text: The bust becomes a sensation, and Egypt demands its return. In 1933 Göring considers giving it back; Hitler refuses: 'I will never relinquish the head of the Queen.'

Title: Found in a salt mine
Text: Hidden from the bombing, the bust is moved to a salt mine, where the US Army finds it in March 1945.

Title: On display in Wiesbaden
Text: The bust is shown at the US Central Collecting Point in Wiesbaden before returning to West Berlin in 1956.

Title: Back on Museum Island
Text: The bust returns to the rebuilt Neues Museum. Egypt continues to demand it back; Berlin cites the 1913 protocol.

Title: Made for the royal palace
Text: Royal guilds cast brass plaques and heads that record the history and rituals of the Benin court.

Title: Looted by British forces
Text: A British naval 'punitive expedition' attacks Benin City, deposes Oba Ovonramwen and takes thousands of objects from the palace.

Title: Sold in London
Text: Many pieces are sold by the British authorities and end up in museums across Europe and the United States, mainly in Germany.

Title: One of the largest collections
Text: Berlin's Ethnological Museum builds up one of the two largest Benin collections in the world, next to the British Museum.

Title: Ownership transferred
Text: Germany signs a joint declaration with Nigeria and transfers ownership of over 1,100 Benin objects in its public collections.

Title: First objects return
Text: Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock hands over a first group of 20 bronzes in Abuja. Others remain in Germany on long-term loan.

Title: The founding queen
Text: Princess Ngonnso founds the Nso kingdom; after her death a cowrie-covered figure is made in her honour.

Title: Taken during a colonial campaign
Text: The figure is taken during military operations of the German colonial army in the grasslands, led by officer Kurt von Pavel.

Title: Donated to the Berlin museum
Text: Von Pavel donates the figure to Berlin's Ethnological Museum. For the Nso, her disappearance leaves a spiritual void.

Title: Found again
Text: Nso scholar Bongasu Tanla Kishani recognises the figure in the Dahlem museum; it is confirmed as Ngonnso in 1988.

Title: Decades of campaigning
Text: Restitution requests in 1998 and 2008 go unanswered. Activists including Sylvie Njobati campaign under the slogan Bring Back Ngonnso.

Title: Return agreed
Text: The Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation authorises Ngonnso's return. The museum decides she will not be exhibited again before going home.

Title: Still waiting
Text: As of early 2025 the handover had not yet taken place.

Title: Punitive expedition
Text: A German naval expedition launched for Hernsheim & Co destroys houses and boats on Luf and kills inhabitants.

Title: Built by the survivors
Text: The men of Luf build a large ocean-going outrigger boat.

Title: Too few to launch it
Text: The islanders plan to use the boat for the sea burial of their leader Labenan, but too few people remain to launch it.

Title: Bought for Berlin
Text: Max Thiel of Hernsheim & Co buys the boat and sells it to Berlin's Museum für Völkerkunde. How the purchase took place is still not fully documented.

Title: Arrives in Berlin
Text: The boat reaches the museum and is later shown in Berlin-Dahlem.

Title: A public debate
Text: Historian Götz Aly's book Das Prachtboot argues the boat is colonial loot, as it goes on display in the new Humboldt Forum.

Title: Research and dialogue
Text: The museum says its provenance research is not concluded and has contacted the National Museum of Papua New Guinea.

Title: A giant lives
Text: Giraffatitan, one of the largest sauropods, lives in what is now southeastern Tanzania.

Title: Bones on the path
Text: Local workers show German engineer Bernhard Sattler huge bones near Tendaguru Hill, in the colony of German East Africa.

Title: Colonial expedition
Text: Berlin's Natural History Museum digs around a hundred quarries. Local porters carry the fossils, since pack animals cannot be used because of the tsetse fly.

Title: Shipped from Lindi
Text: Some 250 tons of fossils are carried to the coast and shipped to Germany.

Title: Mounted in Berlin
Text: A composite skeleton is mounted in the Museum für Naturkunde. Remounted in 2007, it is certified as the world's tallest mounted dinosaur skeleton.

Title: Ownership questioned
Text: German and Tanzanian commentators question the museum's claim; Tanzania has not made an official return request. The museums prefer research cooperation.

Title: Guardians of the gate
Text: A pair of sphinxes guards the southern gate of the Hittite capital.

Title: Taken for restoration
Text: Both sphinxes are brought to Berlin in fragments to be restored.

Title: One goes back
Text: The better-preserved sphinx is returned to Turkey and shown in the Istanbul Archaeology Museum.

Title: One stays in Berlin
Text: The second sphinx is displayed in the Pergamonmuseum for more than 70 years.

Title: Pressure from Ankara
Text: Turkey's culture minister demands the sphinx back; news reports say he threatened the German excavation permit at Hattusa. In May 2011 both sides agree on the transfer.

Title: Reunited at home
Text: The sphinx is returned and placed with its pair in the Boğazköy Museum near the original gate. Germany calls it a gesture of friendship, not restitution.
